l: Gog's invasion of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Gog's invasion of Israel is foretold for the latter years: Gog and many peoples ride from the far north like a storm to seize plunder and prey from a secure, restored people, while the LORD says he brings Gog so nations will know him.

l: God's judgment on Gog, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The LORD executes judgment on Gog when he attacks Israel: wrath causes a great shaking, mountains fall and walls collapse, men turn swords on each other, and pestilence, blood, rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur strike, so the LORD is magnified and known among many nations.

l: valley of Hamon Gog, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_a burial place [for Gog and his multitude] The valley of Hamon Gog is the burial place the Lord GOD gives to Gog in Israel, located in the valley of those who pass through on the east of the sea, where it will stop travelers. Gog and all his multitude are buried there, and it receives its name from this. Bones found by searchers are marked and buried there, and a city will be called Hamonah.

The nations will know that the Lord is the LORD, the Holy One in Israel, and will see his judgment and the hand he has laid on them. They will also learn that Israel went into captivity for its iniquity and trespass, not because of any weakness of God. The Lord will be shown holy among Israel in the sight of many nations.

l: birds and animals (of Gog's slaughter), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Birds of every sort and animals of the field are given Gog and his hordes to be devoured. They are summoned to assemble from every side and eat meat and drink blood until full and drunk at the Lord's table.

l: great sacrifice (the feast on the mountains of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_location mountains of Israel The Lord GOD calls the great sacrifice he prepares on the mountains of Israel, where birds and animals will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth. The feast includes rams, lambs, goats, bulls, fatlings of Bashan, and horses, charioteers, mighty men, and men of war.

l: burial of Gog's army (cleansing the land), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A seven-month burial of Gog's multitude by Israel's people to cleanse the land, bringing them fame when the Lord is glorified; afterward, permanent workers search for remaining bones, marking each until undertakers bury them in the valley of Hamon Gog.

l: Israel's captivity, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Israel's captivity resulted from the house of Israel's iniquity and trespass against the Lord GOD, who hid his face, delivering them to adversaries and the sword. He promises mercy, reversing the captivity, gathering them from enemy lands, and leaving none captive.

l: the man with the measuring reed (guide), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The man with the measuring reed is a guide who appears bronze-like, holding a line of flax and a measuring reed, and leads Ezekiel (the narrator, called Son of man) through the temple vision. In Chapter 40 he stands in the gate, guides the speaker through the outer and inner courts, measures gates, courts, and porches, and explains the priests' rooms. In Chapter 41 he measures the nave, posts, walls, side rooms, and inner room, naming the most holy place and the wooden altar as the table before the LORD. In Chapter 42 he leads the speaker to the north rooms, explains their holiness and the priests' rules, then exits by the east gate and measures all four sides of the surrounding area. In Chapter 47 he leads Ezekiel out the northern gate to the east gate, measures a thousand cubits at a time, has him pass through the waters at each depth, and explains where they go.

l: east gate, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The east gate is a gate facing east, the first gate measured in the vision. The man climbs its steps and measures its thresholds, lodges, porch, posts and opening. It is fifty cubits long, with a ten-cubit opening, three side rooms on each side, closed windows, and palm trees on each post. Later, the glory of the God of Israel arrives from the east and enters the house through it. Finally, it is shut on the six working days, opened on the Sabbath and new moon, and opened for the prince's free will offering, staying open until evening.

l: north gate of outer court, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The north gate of the outer court faces north, fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide like the east gate, with matching lodges, posts, arches, windows and palms; seven steps ascend to it, and an inner gate faces it a hundred cubits away.

l: south gate of outer court, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The south gate of the outer court is a measured gateway, fifty by twenty-five cubits, with windows all around, arches, and palm-decorated posts. Reached by seven steps, it lies one hundred cubits from the inner court's south gate.

l: outer court, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The outer court is a space in a temple vision, surrounding the inner court. In Chapter 40 the guide shows the speaker a pavement all around it, with thirty rooms, lying beside the gates as the lower pavement; one hundred cubits separate the lower gate from the inner court on the east and north. In Chapter 42 the speaker is led north into it, finding rooms fifty cubits long, and priests must change garments before entering.

l: inner court, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A square inner court, one hundred cubits each side, entered by south, east, and north gates of equal measure, each with eight steps; the altar stands before the house within it, alongside rooms for singers and priests.

l: inner gates, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The inner gates (south, east, north) share identical measurements: fifty cubits long, twenty-five wide, with lodges, posts, arches, windows and palm trees. Arches face the outer court, each gate is reached by eight steps, and a washing room for burnt offerings stands by the posts.

l: sacrificial tables, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Sacrificial tables are eight tables in the gate porch, four on each side, used for slaughtering burnt, sin and trespass offerings. Four are cut stone, a cubit and a half square and one cubit high, holding slaughter instruments. Hooks a hand width long are fixed within, and offering meat lies on them.

l: sons of Zadok, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The sons of Zadok are the Levitical priests, holy offspring of Zadok who stand near the LORD and minister to the God of Israel. Their defining distinction is faithfulness: they kept the duty of the sanctuary when Israel went astray, so they alone may come near to offer the fat and blood, enter the sanctuary, and approach the LORD's table. The records unfold from their conduct to their role. First, they eat the most holy things in the holy rooms and must not enter the outer court until they lay aside their holy ministering garments and put on other garments before approaching the people. Next, they receive a young bull for a sin offering, cast salt on offerings, and from the eighth day make the people's burnt and peace offerings. They are then commended for faithfulness, bound by regulations on dress, hair, wine, marriage, teaching, judging, and the dead, and they teach the people holy from common. Their inheritance is the LORD himself, with a holy portion of land for their houses and the sanctuary; a priest also applies sin offering blood to the door posts, altar ledge corners, and inner court gate posts.

l: measurements of the temple, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The temple's measurements are given with a reed of six cubits, each a cubit and a hand width. Chapter 40 sets the wall at one reed thick and high, gates at fifty by twenty-five cubits, and courts and gate distances at one hundred cubits. Chapter 41 then details the nave (twenty by forty), inner room (twenty by twenty), six-cubit house wall, four-cubit side rooms, and a one-hundred-cubit temple length.

l: vision of the new temple, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A vision given to Ezekiel, under the LORD's hand, in the twenty-fifth year of captivity, fourteen years after the city was struck. On a very high mountain in Israel he sees a city-like structure: gates, courts, offering tables, priests' rooms, and porch, and is commanded to declare it to Israel.

The nave is a temple chamber forty cubits long and twenty wide, with a ten-cubit entrance, six-cubit posts on each side, and squared door posts. Its face resembles the temple's; its doors bear cherubim and palm trees, with a wooden threshold on the porch outside.

l: most holy place, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The most holy place is the inner room, measured by a guide after going inward: twenty cubits long and wide, located before the nave, and named so to the narrator.

l: side rooms (of the house), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The side rooms are chambers ringing the house, each four cubits wide, arranged in three stories of thirty rooms and set into the house wall without penetrating it. They widen on higher levels as the walls narrow, reached by climbing through the middle level. Doors face an open area five cubits wide, north and south.

l: separate place (behind the temple), The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_located west of the temple [with a building before it] The building before the separate place on the west side is seventy cubits wide with walls five cubits thick, and ninety cubits long. The separate place and the building with its walls together measure one hundred cubits long. The separate place's east face is counted as one hundred cubits wide with the temple.

Cherubim are carved figures in the house, alternating with palm trees on the walls from ground to above the door. Each has two faces: a man's toward the palm tree on one side, a young lion's toward the other. They also appear on the nave's doors.
A wooden altar, three cubits high and two cubits long, with wooden corners, base and walls; the guide identifies it to the narrator as the table before the LORD.

l: holy rooms (north and south rooms), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The holy rooms are north and south chambers set apart as holy, where priests eat and store the most holy offerings (meal, sin and trespass offerings) near the LORD. Chapter 42 describes the north building: a hundred cubits long, fifty wide, with a north door and three stories of galleries, the upper rooms shorter. Chapter 46 shows priests boiling trespass and sin offerings and baking meal offerings at the back, so the people in the outer court are not sanctified.

l: most holy things (offerings), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The most holy things, including the meal offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering, are eaten by the priests and laid in the holy rooms. The place is called holy for this reason.

l: priestly garments and grooming regulations, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Regulations for priests in Chapter 44: inside the inner court gates they wear only linen garments, turbans, and trousers, with no wool or anything causing sweat. Before entering the outer court they change and leave ministering garments in holy rooms, so as not to sanctify the people. Hair is neither shaved nor long; wine and marriage limits also apply.

l: walls and enclosure (500-cubit wall), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A square wall enclosure, five hundred cubits long and wide, separates the holy from the common; it surrounds the measured area, with a wall by the eastern court's rooms extending fifty cubits.

l: measurement of the surrounding area, The Book of Ezekiel
s: measures_per_side 500 reeds [east, north, south and west sides] After finishing the inner house, the guide leads the speaker out by the east gate and measures all around with the measuring reed. The east, north, south, and west sides each measure five hundred reeds, so the area is measured on all four sides.

l: separation between holy and common, The Book of Ezekiel
s: separates holy from common [effected by the surrounding wall] The wall around the five-hundred-cubit square exists to make a separation between that which is holy and that which is common. The priests' changing of garments before approaching the people reflects the same distinction.

l: the glory of the God of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The glory of the God of Israel approaches from the east with a voice like many waters, illuminating the earth, enters the house through the east-facing gate, and fills it, matching earlier visions including Chebar's.

l: the altar, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The altar is a precisely measured structure with a base, ledges, an upper altar of four cubits, four horns, a twelve-cubit square hearth, a fourteen-cubit square ledge, and east-facing steps. It is meant for burnt offerings and blood sprinkling, and after seven days of cleansing and atonement it is consecrated.

The guide, who speaks to the narrator, brings him through the entry to the holy rooms for the priests and explains their use. He then leads him through the outer court past its four corners and explains that the corner structures are boiling houses.

l: altar consecration offerings, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A seven-day altar consecration ritual for atonement, purification and consecration. It opens with a young bull sin offering whose blood marks the horns, ledge corners and border, the bull burned outside the sanctuary. Daily goat, young bull and ram offerings follow, without defect, with salt; on the eighth day regular burnt and peace offerings begin.

The Levites are a group of ministers of the house who went astray after idols when Israel went astray. Because of this, they bear their iniquity and shame and are barred from priestly office and from coming near the holy and most holy things. Instead they serve in the sanctuary, overseeing the gates, killing the burnt offering and sacrifice for the people, and performing all the house's service. They are then given a portion of land, twenty-five thousand by ten thousand cubits, for twenty rooms, alongside the priests' border. They may not sell or exchange it, since it is holy to the LORD.

l: foreigners (uncircumcised in heart and flesh), The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_barred_from sanctuary (the LORD's house) [including foreigners among the children of Israel] Foreigners uncircumcised in heart and flesh were brought by Israel into the sanctuary when the bread, fat, and blood were offered, profaning the house and breaking the covenant. The LORD decrees that no such foreigner among the children of Israel shall enter his sanctuary.

The prince is a leader figure in the records, defined by land, worship duties, and responsibility to the people. In Chapter 45 he receives land on both sides of the holy allotment and city possession, from west to east border, and is forbidden to oppress the people. He must provide burnt, meal, sin, peace, and drink offerings at feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths, including a Passover sin offering bull for himself and the people. In Chapter 46 he enters by the east gate's porch on Sabbaths and new moons, worships at the threshold, and leaves the same way. He sits there to eat bread before the LORD, may give free will offerings, goes in and out with the people at feasts, and may not seize the people's inheritance. In Chapter 48 he is given the remainder of the land around the Levites' and city possessions, between Judah and Benjamin.

l: east gate of the sanctuary, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The sanctuary's outer east gate, facing east, is shown shut. It must stay unopened and unentered by any man because the LORD, God of Israel, entered by it; only the prince may sit in it to eat bread, using the porch.

l: sanctuary (the LORD's house), The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_filled_with the LORD's glory The LORD's house is filled with the LORD's glory, seen from the north gate. Its ordinances, laws, entrances, and exits are to be carefully marked. It has been profaned by foreigners and is now to be served only by the appointed Levites at its gates and the sons of Zadok within, with inner and outer courts and holy rooms.

l: sanctuary (in the holy portion), The Book of Ezekiel
s: The sanctuary belongs to the LORD and is most holy, set within the holy portion offered to the LORD. It occupies a 500 by 500 square with fifty cubits of pasture around it. Chapter 45 places it by the priests' portion; chapter 48 locates it in the offering's middle, beside Judah's border and the prince's land.

l: just weights and measures, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A set of standard weights and measures: the LORD requires just balances, ephah and bath. Both are one measure, a tenth of a homer; the shekel is twenty gerahs, and the mina sixty shekels.

l: offering of grain, oil and lamb, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A required contribution from all the people of the land for the prince: a sixth of an ephah from a homer of wheat and barley, a tenth of a bath of oil from the cor, and one lamb per two hundred of the flock. It supplies meal, burnt, and peace offerings to make atonement.

l: sacrifices (burnt, meal, sin, peace, drink offerings), The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_purpose atonement for the house of Israel [prepared by the prince] The prince is to provide these offerings at feasts, new moons, Sabbaths, and appointed feasts to make atonement for the house of Israel. During the seven days of Passover, daily offerings are seven bulls, seven rams, and a male goat for a sin offering, with a meal offering of an ephah per bull and ram and a hin of oil per ephah.

l: cleansing of the sanctuary (first month), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A ritual to cleanse the sanctuary, held on the first day of the first month. A priest takes a young bull without defect and puts its sin-offering blood on the house's door posts, the altar ledge's four corners, and the inner court gate posts. The rite is repeated on the seventh day for those who err or are simple, making atonement for the house.

Passover is a seven-day feast held from the fourteenth day of the first month, requiring unleavened bread. The prince provides a sin offering bull on the first day, then daily burnt offerings of seven bulls and seven rams, a male goat sin offering, and oil-mixed meal offerings. A similar feast follows in the seventh month.

l: priests (of the temple), The Book of Ezekiel
s: prepare_for_prince burnt offering [also peace offerings] The priests prepare the prince's burnt offering and peace offerings. They use the holy rooms on the north side to boil the trespass and sin offerings and bake the meal offering so these are not carried into the outer court to sanctify the people.

l: people of the land, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The people of the land are worshipers who bow at the inner court's east gate door on Sabbaths and new moons; at appointed feasts they enter by the north or south gate and exit by the opposite, walking straight, with the prince among them.

l: outer court, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The guide brings the narrator out into the outer court and leads him past its four corners. The priests are to keep the sacrificial portions from being carried out into it, so that the people are not sanctified by them.

l: corner courts, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Four identical enclosed courts, each forty by thirty cubits, sit one in each corner of the outer court; a surrounding wall encloses them, with boiling places built beneath the walls all around.

l: boiling houses, The Book of Ezekiel
s: is_used_by ministers of the house [to boil the people's sacrifice] The guide identifies the boiling places in the corner courts as boiling houses. There the ministers of the house boil the sacrifices of the people.

has_prince_burnt_offering six lambs and a ram [without defect] On the Sabbath the east gate of the inner court is opened. The prince's burnt offering that day is six lambs and a ram without defect, with a meal offering of an ephah for the ram, as much as he can give for the lambs, and a hin of oil to an ephah.

l: new moon, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_prince_burnt_offering young bull, six lambs, and a ram [without defect] The east gate is opened on the day of the new moon, and the people worship at its door. The prince's offering is a young bull, six lambs, and a ram, all without defect, with an ephah of meal for the bull and for the ram and a hin of oil to an ephah.

l: burnt offering, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Burnt offerings are prescribed for the Sabbath, the new moon, and the prince's free will offerings, always of animals without defect. The priests prepare them for the prince, and a lamb a year old is offered daily.

l: meal offering, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_amount_for_ram ephah [with a hin of oil to an ephah] Meal offerings accompany the animal offerings: an ephah for the bull or ram, as much as the prince is able for the lambs, and a hin of oil to an ephah. The priests bake the meal offering in the holy rooms to keep it from the outer court.

l: daily continual burnt offering, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A daily burnt offering to the LORD: a year-old lamb without defect prepared each morning, accompanied by a sixth of an ephah of meal offering with a third of a hin of oil, established as a perpetual ordinance.

l: prince's inheritance laws, The Book of Ezekiel
s: Chapter 46 laws on the prince's inheritance: a gift to his sons is permanent and remains their possession; a gift to a servant returns to the prince in the year of liberty; the prince may not seize the people's inheritance, giving sons from his own.

l: river (flowing from the temple), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A river flowing eastward from beneath the temple threshold, deepening every thousand cubits from ankle-deep to too deep to cross. It descends through the Arabah into the Dead Sea, healing its waters and giving life to every creature, though its swamps and marshes stay salt.

l: trees (along the river), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Many food-bearing trees line both banks of the river flowing from the temple. Their leaves never wither and their fruit never fails, bearing new fruit monthly because the waters issue from the sanctuary. The fruit serves as food and the leaves bring healing.

l: the sea (Dead Sea), The Book of Ezekiel
s: A sea receiving the river's waters, which will be made to flow out and heal it; fish will multiply greatly and fishermen will spread nets from En Gedi to En Eglaim, though its swamps and marshes stay unhealed, given up to salt.

l: aliens (strangers among Israel), The Book of Ezekiel
s: Aliens living among Israel and raising children there are regarded as native-born among the children of Israel, and so share in the inheritance, receiving a portion in whichever tribe they live.

l: borders of the land, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The borders of the land are defined on four sides in Chapter 47. The north runs from the great sea via Hethlon to Zedad, Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim, Hazer Hatticon and Hazar Enon at Damascus's border; the east is the Jordan; the south runs from Tamar to Meriboth Kadesh and the brook; the west is the great sea.

Dan is a tribe, named first in Chapter 48, receiving one portion at the far northern end beside Hethlon, Hamath's entrance, and Hazar Enan at Damascus's border; it also names one of three east city gates.

l: tribes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel
s: The tribes each receive one portion running east to west, and those who labor in the city out of all the tribes cultivate the city's land. The twelve city gates are named after the tribes, with Joseph, Levi and Benjamin among them.

The priests are sanctified sons of Zadok who kept the LORD's instruction and did not go astray when Israel and the Levites did. They receive a most holy offering, twenty-five thousand by ten thousand, with the sanctuary in its middle, bordering the Levites' portion.

l: holy offering, The Book of Ezekiel
s: A holy offering dedicated to the LORD, set apart for the priests with the sanctuary at its middle. Measuring 25,000 by 25,000 reeds with the Levites' portion and the city's possession, it lies beside Judah's border.

A square city set in the middle of a leftover strip of land for common use, dwelling and pasture. It measures 4,500 reeds per side, has 250 reeds of pasture around it, and an 18,000 circumference. Twelve gates, three per side, bear tribal names. Workers from all the tribes farm its land for food. From that day it is named 'The LORD is there.'

l: tribal portions, The Book of Ezekiel
s: has_shape strips from east side to west side Twelve tribal portions are laid out as east-west strips, seven from Dan to Judah in the north and five from Benjamin to Gad in the south. Each tribe has one portion, and Gad's border forms the southern boundary of the land.

Obadiah's vision records the LORD's judgment against Edom, also called Esau, whose pride in its high rocky dwelling leads it to think no one can bring it down. The LORD says he will make Edom small, bring it down from its heights, and destroy its wise men and mighty men, including those of Teman. Edom is condemned for violence against its brother Jacob: it stood aside while strangers plundered Jerusalem, and it rejoiced, seized wealth, and cut off escapees. The day of the LORD is near for all the nations, and what they have done will return on their own heads. Mount Zion will have those who escape, the house of Jacob will be a fire consuming the house of Esau, and the possessions of Esau and other lands will be taken, ending with the kingdom belonging to the LORD.

Edom, also called Esau, is told it has been made small and despised, and that pride in its high rocky dwelling has deceived it. Its allies and friends betray it, its wise and mighty men are destroyed, and it is cut off forever for violence against Jacob and for standing aside, rejoicing, and plundering when Jerusalem fell. The house of Esau becomes stubble burned by Jacob, with none remaining, and its mountain is possessed by those of the South and judged by saviors from Mount Zion.

The LORD speaks against Edom, saying he will bring it down even from among the stars and destroy its wise men and understanding. He declares that the day of the LORD is near for all the nations and that deeds will be repaid. He has spoken that none will remain of the house of Esau, and the kingdom will be his.

Jacob is Edom's brother, against whom Edom committed violence, and whose Jerusalem and children of Judah suffered disaster and plunder. In the end the house of Jacob will possess its possessions and be a fire, with the house of Joseph a flame, that devours the house of Esau.

l: Mount Zion, The Book of Obadiah
s: Mount Zion is where there will be those who escape, and it will be holy. Saviors will go up on Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Obadiah
s: The day of the LORD is said to be near for all the nations. On it, as they have done will be done to them, and their deeds will return on their own heads.

The nations are told that an ambassador has been sent among them to rise up against Edom in battle, and Edom is made small among them. The day of the LORD is near for all the nations, who as they drank on God's holy mountain will drink continually, swallow down, and be as though they had not been.
